title: SRE guidelines: SLOs, error budgets, capacity planning, reliability initiatives and runbooks
author: Daniel Kim
summary: Company-wide SRE guidance consolidating SLO definitions, error budget policy, capacity planning best practices, reliability initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling, and canonical runbooks. This doc is intended as the single source of truth for oncall teams, service owners, and platform engineers.
body:
Overview:

This document defines Redwood Inference’s standard approach to service-level objectives (SLOs) and error budgets, capacity planning and forecasting, reliability improvement initiatives, incident review standards, operational tooling expectations, and canonical runbooks. It applies to all production-facing services and platform components (hosted API, dedicated control plane, private deployments, runtime, scheduling, and observability pipelines).

Key goals:
- Ensure consistent SLO definitions across services so business and engineering have a shared contract about reliability.
- Maintain predictable capacity and cost by standardized forecasting and autoscaling guidelines.
- Drive continuous reliability improvements through prioritized initiatives and clear post-incident learning.
- Make runbooks actionable and testable so oncall can restore service quickly and safely.

1) SLOs and Error Budgets

High-level SLO guidance:
- Every externally visible service must publish at least one availability SLO and one latency SLO, where applicable. Internal infra services should publish health and throughput SLOs.
- SLOs are defined at the customer-visible API level (e.g., /v1/generate, /v1/embeddings) and must include precise measurement windows and denominators.

Canonical SLO templates (examples):
| SLO name | Target | Measurement window | Objective | Denominator | Notes |
|---|---:|---|---|---|---|
| Hosted API availability | 99.95% | 30d rolling | Successful HTTP 2xx responses for text endpoints | total requests | Excludes scheduled maintenance windows with >=72h notice |
| Inference latency (p99) | <= 350ms | 30d rolling | End-to-end server processing latency (excl. network egress) | successful requests | Separate SLOs for small and large models if latency profiles differ |
| Control plane readiness | 99.9% | 30d rolling | API responses for control-plane endpoints | total control-plane requests | Includes model management and allocation endpoints |

Error budget policy:
- Error budget = 1 - SLO. Teams track budget consumption on a rolling 30d window.
- Burn thresholds and actions: 
  1. Normal (0-25% burn): Proceed with normal releases. Monitor.
  2. Elevated (25-50% burn): Increase monitoring cadence, delay non-critical rollouts. Notify platform SRE.
  3. High (50-80% burn): Freeze feature releases for affected service(s); require oncall handoff for any changes; open a reliability ticket.
  4. Exhausted (>=80% burn or SLO violated): Declare an error-budget incident, halt all non-critical changes until recovery and a mitigation plan are in place. Schedule postmortem within 5 business days.
- Exception process: Product or executive-requested intentional changes that consume budget (e.g., load tests) must be pre-authorized and time-boxed with a written approval in the change log.

SLO measurement & tooling requirements:
- Metrics sources: primary measurement must be from the service’s production telemetry (Prometheus/OTel metrics, request logs). Synthetic checks may be used as secondary signals.
- Labels/metadata: Every SLO metric must include service, route, region, model-version (if applicable), and environment tags.
- Dashboards: Each SLO must have a canonical dashboard with 30d, 7d, and 1d views and a burn-rate chart.

2) Capacity planning

Goals and cadence:
- Provide capacity headroom to meet SLOs under forecasted growth and typical p95/p99 traffic spikes.
- Quarterly capacity planning cycle with monthly checkpoints for high-growth services.

Forecasting process:
1. Baseline: Use historical telemetry (90-365 day window) to compute baseline RPS, average tokens/sec, and peak concurrency by region and model class.
2. Growth assumptions: Product/BD owners provide expected growth rates and planned events (marketing releases, model launches).
3. Safety margin: Apply a default 40% safety margin for production-hosted endpoints; reduce to 20% for Dedicated customers with reserved capacity and known traffic patterns.
4. Capacity model: Convert forecasted load to GPU/CPU and memory requirements using per-model perf profiles and batch-sizing assumptions. Include queuing latency impact.
5. Validation: Run synthetic load tests and perf bench to validate estimates at least once per cycle.

Autoscaling & headroom rules:
- Target utilization: 60-70% average GPU utilization for pooled serving nodes to preserve headroom for spikes. For dedicated/reserved clusters target 70-80%.
- Scale-up latency: Configure autoscalers to scale fast for vertical spikes (scale-up target within 90s) while scaling down conservatively (cooldown >= 5 minutes).
- Burst capacity: Maintain a short-duration burst pool (10-15% of fleet) to absorb sudden traffic spikes without SLO drops.

Capacity runbook checklist (quarterly):
- Review top 20 endpoints by traffic and their SLOs.
- Update perf profiles after any model or runtime changes.
- Re-run load tests for critical routes.
- Confirm available spare capacity and burst pool size.
- Validate alarms and autoscaler runbooks.

3) Reliability initiatives and prioritization

Typical initiative types:
- Latency optimizations (runtime kernel improvements, batching improvements).
- Cost vs. reliability tuning (quantization profiles and routing policies).
- Observability upgrades (traces per request, distributed sampling, improved SLO dashboards).
- Operational automation (self-healing scripts, autoscaler improvements).

Prioritization framework:
- Rank initiatives by expected reduction in error budget burn, customer impact, and engineering effort (RICE-style with reliability-focused scoring).
- Maintain a quarterly Reliability Roadmap owned by SRE with delivery milestones.

Example OKR for SRE reliability quarter:
- Objective: Reduce p99 latency-violation error-budget burn by 50% across hosted API.
  - KR1: Deploy continuous KV-prefix caching to 80% of routes (reduce per-token compute by 12%).
  - KR2: Tune batching heuristics to reduce p99 CPU stalls by 25%.
  - KR3: Add targeted synthetic tests for top 10 customer flows and onboard to alerting.

4) Incident review standards and postmortems

Severity levels and owner expectations:
- Sev-1 (SEV1): Customer-visible outage impacting >5% of traffic or critical platform control-plane failures. Immediate pager and all-hands. Postmortem required within 3 business days.
- Sev-2 (SEV2): Partial degradation or significant latency increases affecting <5% but with detectable SLO impact. Pager to primary oncall and secondary. Postmortem required within 7 business days.
- Sev-3 (SEV3): Minor issues, operational work, or non-urgent degradations. Track in tickets, include in monthly reliability review.

Postmortem structure (required fields):
- Title, incident ID, severity, start/end timestamps (UTC).
- Impact summary (customers affected, endpoints, regions).
- Root cause analysis (5 Whys), timeline of events, mitigations, and detection path.
- Metrics and graphs showing SLO burn, latency, error rates, and capacity during incident.
- Action items (owner, priority, due date).
- Roll-forward plan and verification steps.
- Learnings and systemic recommendations (link to related RFC or ADR if applicable).

Review process:
- All SEV1/SEV2 postmortems must be reviewed by SRE leads and product owners within 5 business days.
- Action items must be tracked in a reliability backlog and reported in the monthly reliability review.

5) Operational tooling and observability expectations

Minimum tooling for service owners:
- Metrics: Prometheus (or managed backend) metrics with standard labels described in the SLO section.
- Tracing: Distributed traces (OpenTelemetry) with sampled traces for 1 in 50 requests at minimum for high-volume endpoints; 1 in 5 for suspect flows.
- Logging: Structured request logs with correlation IDs and model/version metadata.
- Alerting: Alert on SLO burn-rate (15m, 1h), p95/p99 latency breaches, and error-rate spikes. Use PagerDuty policies per severity.
- Synthetic checks: Canary synthetic tests per route and region (min 3 per region) and canary-based automatic rollback for deploys that exceed thresholds.

Operational integrations:
- Slack channels for runbook-driven incident comms, with automated status updates from the status page.
- Incident timeline recorded in the issue tracker (JIRA).
- Runbook exercises (game-days) scheduled twice yearly per critical service.

6) Canonical runbooks (templates & examples)

Every service must maintain a short, actionable runbook for the top 3 failure modes. Runbooks follow this template:
- Title: one-line description
- Symptoms: observable signals (metrics/alerts) that indicate this failure mode
- Impact: what customer-visible functionality is affected
- Immediate mitigation steps (ordered, numbered, with CLI/console commands)
- Rollback/compensating actions
- Post-incident verification checks
- Owner and escalation path

Example runbook: "Inference-High-Latency (p99)"
1. Symptoms:
   - p99 latency > 350ms for >3 minutes on /v1/generate in region-us-west
   - Error rate stable but queue length increasing
2. Immediate mitigation:
   1) Redirect new requests to unaffected region via routing console: `redwood route set --service hosted-api --region us-east`
   2) Scale up serving pool for region-us-west: `kubectl scale deployment hosted-runtime --replicas=12 -n hosted-us-west` (confirm capacity with `kubectl top pods`)
   3) Enable degraded serving profile for large models: update config `model_profiles: large_model: max_seq=512, batch_size=8`
3. Verification:
   - p99 latency returns below 350ms for 5 consecutive 1-minute buckets
   - Queue length below threshold and error budget burn rate reduced
4. Post-incident:
   - Open postmortem if SLO violated or error budget >= 50% consumed.
   - Schedule replay/load test for the failing flow and update perf profiles.

Runbook testing and hygiene:
- Each runbook must be exercised at least once per quarter (game-day).
- Runbooks must include tested CLI/console commands and have no interactive-only steps.
- Maintain a runbook ownership table with oncall rotation owners.

7) Ownership, escalation, and governance

Ownership model:
- Service owner: Product-engineering team that owns feature/route and SLO. Responsible for SLO definitions, runbook maintenance, and executing reliability actions.
- Platform SRE: Ownership for platform-wide reliability initiatives, capacity planning, autoscaler rules, and cross-team incident coordination.
- Observability team: Ownership for dashboards, traces, and alerting primitives.

Escalation path:
1. Primary oncall (service owner)
2. Platform SRE (if systemic or cross-service)
3. Eng SRE lead / oncall manager
4. CTO/VP Eng for customer-impacting or legal/compliance-impacting incidents

Governance & review cadence:
- Quarterly SLO review with product and SRE to validate targets and make adjustments.
- Monthly reliability council to review postmortem action-item progress and prioritize initiatives.

Appendix: Templates and quick references

- SLO naming convention: `<service>.<endpoint>.<metric>.<region>` (e.g., hosted-api.v1-generate.availability.us-west)
- Example alert thresholds:
  - p99 latency breach: alert if p99 > target for 3 consecutive 1m buckets.
  - Burn-rate alert: alert when 24h burn rate >= 5x baseline for 15m.
- Contact matrix: includes rotation owners, SRE leads, oncall PD policy, and escalation Slack channels (maintained in team wiki).

Document maintenance:
- Owners must review and update this doc quarterly or after any significant incident or platform change.
- Major changes to SLO targets require approval from product leadership and a signed change log entry.

End of document.
